chapters.name: Chapter 1: Picking and testing your hustle

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Matching a side hustle to your skills
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List side hustle ideas that fit your skills, time and money.
This lesson builds toward: Given your skills, time, starting money and rules, you will choose a side hustle and check whether it needs a license or is limited by your conditions, naming where you checked.
The best first side hustle uses skills you already have, needs little money to start, and fits your schedule. If you cooked inside, think meal prep or catering help. If you did maintenance, think small repairs or yard work. If people always ask you to fix their hair, start there.
Ask AI for ideas: "I am good at cooking and cleaning, I have about 10 hours a week, no car, and less than $100 to start. Suggest 10 side hustles I could start in my neighborhood." Then cross out any that do not fit you.
Check your rules first. Parole or probation conditions may limit some work, travel or handling cash. Some trades, like barbering, cosmetology, electrical or contracting, need a state license. Some licenses consider criminal records; your state licensing board's website explains its rules.
Step by step:
- List your skills, time per week and starting money.
- Ask AI for ten ideas that fit.
- Cross out ideas that do not fit your life.
- Check parole or probation conditions.
- Check whether the work needs a state license.
Words to know:
- Side hustle: a small way to earn money on your own, often part time.
- License: official permission from the state or city to do certain work.
Try it now: Ask AI for ten side hustle ideas using your real skills, time and budget. Pick your top two and write what rules or licenses you need to check for each.
You can now pick side hustle ideas that fit your skills and know which rules to check.

check.q: What three things should a good first side hustle fit?
options: Your car, your house and your credit score
The newest trend, a big loan and a website
Your skills, your time and the money you have to start
Your friends' jobs, a license and an office
check.why: A first side hustle uses skills you already have, needs little money and fits your schedule.

check.q: You want to cut hair for money. What do you check first?
options: Whether your state requires a barbering or cosmetology license, and your conditions
Nothing; it is just a side hustle
Only what your friends think
Which clippers are most expensive
check.why: Some trades, like barbering, need a state license, and parole or probation conditions may apply.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Testing if people will pay
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Test demand for your idea in a week without spending money.
This lesson builds toward: Before you spend money on supplies, you will test whether people will pay by talking to ten possible customers and checking others nearby, within one week, spending nothing.
Before buying supplies, find out if people want it. Talk to ten people who could be customers: neighbors, church members, family friends, people at your reentry center. Ask: "Would you pay someone to [service]? How often? What would you expect to pay?"
Look around: are others already doing it nearby? That is good news; it means people pay for it. Ask AI: "What do customers usually complain about with [service]?" Fixing those complaints can be your edge.
Offer one or two jobs at a fair starter price to people you know, and ask them for honest feedback and, if they are happy, a short review or referral.
Step by step:
- Talk to ten possible customers.
- Ask if they would pay, how often and how much.
- Look for others doing it nearby.
- Ask AI what customers usually complain about.
- Do one or two starter jobs and ask for feedback.
Words to know:
- Demand: how many people want something and will pay for it.
- Referral: when a happy customer sends you a new customer.
Try it now: Write the three questions you will ask, then talk to at least five possible customers this week. Write down what they said.
You can now test whether people will pay before you spend money.

options: The price of your supplies
The number of hours you work
Your license number
How many people want something and will pay for it
check.why: Demand is how many people want your service and will pay.

check.q: You want to start a yard work hustle. What is the best first step?
options: Buy a new lawn mower
Ask ten neighbors if they would pay, how often and how much
Print 500 flyers
Set up a website
check.why: Test demand by talking to possible customers before spending money.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Setting your price
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set a price that covers costs, pays you fairly and fits the market.
This lesson builds toward: Given your costs per job, the hours it takes and local prices, you will calculate a price that covers costs, your time and a little extra, with the math checked by hand.
A price has to cover three things: your costs (supplies, bus fare or gas, phone), your time, and a little extra to save or grow. Underpricing feels safe, but it can leave you working for almost nothing.
Example: cleaning an apartment takes 3 hours and $10 in supplies. If you want $20 an hour for your time, that is $60 plus $10, so about $70. Then check: what do others nearby charge? Adjust up or down.
Ask AI to check your math and suggest packages: "I clean apartments. My costs are $10 per job, I want $20 per hour, a job takes 3 hours. Suggest a basic price, a deep-clean price and a weekly discount." Double-check its math yourself.
Step by step:
- Add up costs per job.
- Decide what your hour is worth and multiply by hours.
- Add costs plus time.
- Compare with others nearby.
- Ask AI to suggest packages, then check the math.
Words to know:
- Cost: money you spend to do the job.
- Package: a set of services sold together at one price.
Try it now: Figure your price for one job of your side hustle: costs, time and market check. Ask AI to suggest two packages and check the math.
You can now set a fair price based on costs, time and the market.

check.q: A job takes 4 hours, you want $15 an hour, and supplies cost $8. What is the base price?
check.why: 4 hours times $15 is $60, plus $8 in supplies, which is $68.

check.q: Your base price is $70, but everyone nearby charges about $90 for the same job. What do you do?
options: Drop to $30 to win every job
Keep $70 no matter what
Adjust your price after comparing, since you may be underpricing
Refuse to set a price
check.why: Compare with others nearby and adjust; underpricing can leave you working for almost nothing.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Writing your offer and a flyer with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a clear offer and make a flyer or social post with AI help.
This lesson builds toward: Using an AI assistant and a free design tool, you will write a clear offer and make a flyer or social post, saying what, who, price and how to book, with nothing untrue and no home address.
An offer says what you do, who it is for, the price and how to book. Example: "Apartment cleaning in Eastside. Basic clean $70, deep clean $110. Reliable, careful, references available. Text [phone] to book."
Ask AI: "Write three short versions of an offer for my [service] in [area] at [price]. Friendly and trustworthy. Under 40 words." Pick the one that sounds most like you, and remove anything not true, like "licensed and insured" if you are not.
Make a flyer or post in Canva's free plan or Google Docs. Use a clear headline, two or three benefits, the price and how to contact you. Use a separate business phone number or a free texting number if you can, and never post your home address.
Step by step:
- Write what, who, price and how to book.
- Ask AI for three short versions.
- Pick one and remove anything not true.
- Make a flyer or post with a headline, benefits, price and contact.
- Keep your home address private.
Words to know:
- Offer: a clear statement of what you sell, for whom, at what price.
- Flyer: a one-page printed or digital ad.
Try it now: Use AI to write three versions of your offer, pick one, and make a flyer or social post with it.
You can now write an honest offer and make a simple flyer or post with AI help.

check.q: What four things does a clear offer say?
options: Your name, age, address and story
What you do, who it is for, the price and how to book
Your skills, school, hobbies and goals
Only the price
check.why: A clear offer says what, for whom, the price and how to book.

check.q: You are making a flyer for your cleaning service. Which contact detail do you leave off?
options: Your business phone number
A free texting number
Your first name
Your home address
check.why: Never post your home address; use a business or free texting number.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Getting your first customers safely
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find first customers through people and places you trust, and work safely.
This lesson builds toward: When you look for your first customers, you will plan who and where to tell and how you will work safely, with a list of five people or places and the job agreed in writing.
Your first customers usually come from people who know you: family, friends, church, your reentry program, past co-workers. Tell five people a day what you do and hand them a flyer or send your post.
Post on community boards: libraries, laundromats, community centers and local online groups, following each place's rules. Ask every happy customer for a review or to tell a friend.
Stay safe. Meet new customers in public first or bring someone with you. Get paid the way you agreed, and be careful with apps: never accept an overpayment and send money back, which is a common scam. Write down what each job includes before you start so there is no confusion.
Step by step:
- Tell five people a day about your service.
- Post on community boards and local groups.
- Ask happy customers for reviews and referrals.
- Agree in writing what each job includes and the price.
- Watch for overpayment scams.
Words to know:
- Word of mouth: customers telling other people about you.
- Overpayment scam: a trick where someone pays too much and asks you to send the difference back, then their payment bounces.
Official sources:
- FTC: Fake check scams
Try it now: Write a list of 15 people or places to tell about your hustle. Contact five of them today with your flyer or post.
You can now find first customers through trusted people and places while staying safe.

check.q: Where do most first customers come from?
options: Paid online ads
Strangers in other cities
People who know you, like family, friends and church
Big companies
check.why: First customers usually come from people who already know and trust you.

check.q: A new customer you have never met wants you to come to their home. What is safer?
options: Meet in public first or bring someone with you
Go alone and tell no one
Ask for full payment in gift cards
Share your home address
check.why: Meet in public first or bring someone, and agree on the job in writing.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Tracking money and getting ready for taxes
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Keep a simple money log and know the basics of side hustle taxes.
This lesson builds toward: From your first sale, you will keep a money log and save receipts, and name where to get tax help, recording every dollar in and out.
Track every dollar from day one. A simple money log in Google Sheets or a notebook: date, customer (first name or label), job, money in, money out, and what the money out was for. Keep receipts for supplies, in a folder or as phone photos.
In the U.S., side hustle income is taxable, even cash and even small amounts. Self-employed people may owe self-employment tax and may need to pay estimated taxes during the year. The rules and thresholds change, so check irs.gov or a free tax help program such as VITA before tax time.
If you grow, you may want a business bank account, a business name registration with your city or state, or an EIN. The IRS says an EIN is free from the IRS; beware of websites that charge for one. AI can help you make the money log and explain tax words, but for your actual taxes, use irs.gov or a tax professional.
Step by step:
- Make a money log: date, customer label, job, in, out, what for.
- Save every receipt.
- Add up your income and costs each month.
- Set aside part of each payment for taxes.
- Check irs.gov or a free tax help program before tax time.
Words to know:
- Self-employment tax: U.S. Social Security and Medicare tax for people who work for themselves.
- EIN: Employer Identification Number: a federal tax ID number for a business.
- VITA: Volunteer Income Tax Assistance: free IRS-supported tax help for people who qualify.
Official sources:
- IRS: Get an Employer Identification Number
- IRS: Manage taxes for your gig work
- IRS: Free tax return preparation (VITA)
Try it now: Final task: make your money log and finish your one-page launch sheet: service, rules checked, price, offer, flyer or post, five people or places to tell, and the money log ready for your first sale.
You can now start a side hustle with AI help, find customers safely and track your money for taxes.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Service and rules The service is unclear, or rules and licenses were not checked. Names the service and who it is for, and says which rules or licenses were checked and where. Also notes how the learner confirmed it fits their parole or probation conditions, if they apply. Price No price, or the price does not cover costs. A price that covers costs, time and a little extra, with the math shown. Compared with others nearby and offers a package or two. Offer and flyer Missing price or contact, has untrue claims, or shows a home address. Says what, who, price and how to book, with nothing untrue and no home address. The flyer has a clear headline and two or three benefits and sounds like the learner. First customers Fewer than five people or places listed. Five people or places to tell, and a plan to agree on each job in writing. Includes a safety plan for meeting new customers and avoiding overpayment scams. Money log No money log. A money log ready with date, customer label, job, in, out and what for. Includes a receipts folder and where to get free tax help. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What goes in a side hustle money log?
options: Customers' full names and phone numbers
Only the money you earned
Your bank password
Date, customer label, job, money in, money out and what it was for
check.why: A money log tracks every dollar in and out from day one.

check.q: You earned $300 cash this month from small jobs. What do you do about taxes?
options: Nothing; cash is not taxable
Record it, set part aside, and check irs.gov or VITA before tax time
Spend it before anyone knows
Ask a customer to file for you
check.why: Side hustle income is taxable even in cash, so track it and get trusted tax help.
